args.text:
If you’re a program manager or a federal web developer, odds are someone's dropped what sounds like a dead simple job on your desk: whip up a website for some initiative at your agency. Easy, you reckon. Except the hard yakka usually isn't writing the content or designing the thing. It's getting the security and privacy compliance squared away so you can launch the actual website and keep it ticking over. And for that lot you might have to get a contractor in, or load up your agency’s web team when they're already flat out.

Fair go, it shouldn’t be like that.

## Why Pages?

Pages looks after our fellow federal partners by taking care of the backend and compliance grind for launching and running a website, and doing it like it knows what it's on about, so you can put your know-how where it counts: your content.

- **FedRAMP Certified Platform** Pages is hosted on cloud.gov, a platform whose security and compliance has been checked over and signed off by the FedRAMP Joint Authorization Board. Translation: you can count on your site being fast, reliable, and ready when a surprise rush of traffic comes piling through the door.

- **Easy previews and content approvals** Pages builds draft updates to your site at a special preview URL. So your team can see their changes will come up right before they're pushed to the main site, no nasty surprises, and it's easy as to get the nod from stakeholders on content updates.

[![Diagram of Pages architecture]({{site.baseurl}}/assets/images/pages/how-pages-works-diagram.png)]({{site.baseurl}}/assets/documents/how-pages-works-diagram.pdf)

## Why static websites?

Pages turns out static websites instead of running some more complicated content management system (CMS) like Drupal or WordPress. And static websites have a fair bit going for them:

- **Less complexity and vulnerability:** Skip the traditional CMS and you skip a whole swag of headaches, like nursing server applications along (no PHP or Apache / IIS), on top of database scaling and redundancy. A production-level static site generally needs one simple static file server or service, not dozens of the things. So the whole website's easier to look after and there are fewer holes for the baddies to poke at.

- **Update content without writing code:** Static websites often keep their content in plain old text files that anyone on the team can have a go at. The GitHub editor lets any team member make basic edits to their text files, whether they've written heaps of code or never touched the stuff.

- **Easy to host and maintain:** Hosting static website files on Pages is a piece of piss. Nah, keep it clean: it's dead easy. You can make the most of scaling services like Amazon S3 through Pages, and you only pay for what you use, not a cent more.

- **Fully customizable:** Designers and developers can bend static websites into whatever shape they're after without having to rip out CMS-provided features and defaults first. Static sites will do you for all sorts of sites, from organisation homepages or intranets right through to pre-generated web application program interfaces that show data from a separate server.

result.scope: Issues: flagged phrases, swearing over the cap, US spelling and US words. Warnings: the guide's style rules and swearing density; fidelity to the original (length, names, numbers). Not checked: invented slang.

declined.reason: 'builds out draft updates' is the site generator compiling a preview, not putting something together quickly and roughly
'used to build many types of sites' is a product claim; 'quickly and roughly' undercuts it
flamin' carries exasperation; on 'very easy' in a selling point it reads as a complaint
